summary.text: The ultimate fate of the universe is a question in physical cosmology about how the universe might evolve and eventually end.
Which future is possible depends on the universe's overall shape, how much dark energy it holds, and how that dark energy responds to expansion.
Since 1998, observations of distant supernovas have been read as showing an accelerating expansion, and most cosmologists expect the universe to expand forever.

items.prompt: A universe has so much matter that its space is closed, curved like a sphere. If it had no dark energy, what would gravity eventually do to its expansion?

options.label: Keep it going at a steady, unchanging pace
Stop it, then pull everything back together
Make it speed up until nothing holds together
Freeze the universe in a fixed, static size

items.explain: In a closed universe, gravity eventually stops the expansion and the universe contracts to a final singularity.

items.prompt: Someone argues that a closed universe must always collapse. What does the Lambda-CDM model say about that?

options.label: Collapse is certain once density exceeds the critical value
Dark energy would make the collapse happen sooner
Only an open universe can contain any dark energy
Dark energy's push can keep it expanding forever anyway

items.explain: Dark energy's repulsive force may be enough to keep expansion going forever, even if Ω > 1.

items.prompt: In 1998, astronomers studied supernovas in distant galaxies, expecting gravity to be braking the expansion. What did the observations fit best?

options.label: An expansion that is speeding up
An expansion that is slowing at a steady rate
A universe that stopped expanding long ago
A universe that has started to shrink

items.explain: Starting in 1998, supernova observations were interpreted as consistent with an accelerating expansion, which led theorists to invoke dark energy.

items.prompt: Two theories competed in the mid-1900s: one said the universe began very dense, the other said it stayed statistically unchanged as new matter appeared. Which finding tipped the scales?

options.label: Cepheid stars seen in distant galaxies
Einstein's view of a static universe
The cosmic microwave background radiation, found in 1965
The measurement that space is flat

items.explain: The Big Bang predicts the cosmic microwave background, which the original Steady State theory could not account for.

items.prompt: A galaxy's gravity bends the space right around it. Does that make the whole universe 'closed'?

options.label: Yes, any mass that bends space closes the universe
No, the labels describe overall geometry, not local curving
Yes, but only if the galaxy is large enough
No, because space only bends near black holes

items.explain: Flat, open and closed refer to the overall geometry, not the local curving caused by clumps such as galaxies and stars.

items.prompt: Cosmologists divide the universe's average matter density by a critical density. Which quantity do they get?

options.label: The age of the universe
The rate of expansion
The share of dark energy
The density parameter, omega

items.explain: The density parameter omega is the average matter density divided by a critical value, and it selects the universe's geometry.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?

steps.text: A universe with Ω > 1 is closed.
In a closed universe, gravity eventually stops the expansion and the universe contracts.
Dark energy's repulsive force can only ever make that contraction faster.
So dark energy has no bearing on how a closed universe ends.

paragraphs.heading: A scientific question
paragraphs.text: How the universe will ultimately end is a question for physical cosmology, where theory limits which futures are possible and lets them be weighed against each other. With observational evidence now at hand, it has become a real scientific question rather than one left to myth or theology. Different hypotheses have predicted different futures, including a universe that lasts a finite time or one that lasts forever.

paragraphs.heading: How the question opened
paragraphs.text: Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity, from 1915, made it possible to explore the universe's fate in theory, and it can describe the cosmos on its largest scales. Its equations have several solutions, and each one implies a different ending. Alexander Friedmann found several in 1922, and Georges Lemaître did too in 1927. After Edwin Hubble concluded in 1929 that the universe was expanding, both its start and its possible end became subjects of serious research.

paragraphs.heading: Density sets the shape
paragraphs.text: A key number is the density parameter, omega (Ω): the universe's average density of matter divided by a critical value. If Ω equals 1 the universe is called flat, if it is less than 1 it is open, and if it is more than 1 it is closed. These words describe the geometry of the universe as a whole, not the local bending of spacetime around galaxies or stars. In a closed universe the angles of a triangle add up to more than 180 degrees, and in an open one they add up to less.

paragraphs.heading: Crunch or keep going
paragraphs.text: If the universe held mostly inert matter, each geometry would lead to its own fate, so cosmologists tried to measure Ω, or how quickly the expansion was slowing down. In a closed universe, gravity would eventually halt the expansion, and everything would then contract into a final point called the Big Crunch, the reverse of the Big Bang. Dark energy, however, can push outward hard enough to keep the expansion going forever, even when Ω is above 1.

paragraphs.heading: Where things stand
paragraphs.text: Cosmologists broadly agree that the universe is flat, meaning parallel lines stay parallel, and that it will keep expanding forever. Measurements from the WMAP probe also point to a universe that is flat or very nearly so. Even so, the final outcome depends on the overall shape, how much dark energy there is, and how its density responds as the universe expands. Coming galaxy surveys by three space telescopes, Euclid, Nancy Grace Roman and James Webb, are expected to sharpen our picture of what dark energy is.
